sources.entry: A virtual private network (VPN) extends a private network across a public network and enables users to send and receive data across shared or public networks as if their computing devices were directly connected to the private network.

summary.name: Virtual private network (VPN)
summary.one_liner: A Wikipedia overview of virtual private networks, which extend a private network across a public network using encryption and tunneling protocols.
use_cases: secure off-site access to an office network
connecting a branch office to headquarters or a data center
understanding VPN protocols such as IPsec, OpenVPN and WireGuard
learning how split tunneling affects traffic
encrypting traffic on untrusted Wi-Fi or ISP networks
summary.what_it_does: The article explains what a VPN is: an overlay network that uses encryption and tunneling to carry private network traffic across a public network such as the Internet. It describes topologies including host-to-network, site-to-site, provider-provisioned, mobile, MPLS, VPLS, EVPN and DMVPN. It covers protocols such as IPsec, TLS/SSL, OpenSSH, OpenVPN, SSTP, WireGuard, DTLS and L2TP, with dates and technical details. It also discusses security limits, split tunneling trade-offs, and VPN use in society and by individuals.
notable: Covers many VPN topologies and protocols in one reference
Explains that VPNs do not make users anonymous to their ISP
Notes WireGuard was added to Linux and Android kernels in 2020
Describes split tunneling advantages and DNS leak risks
caveats: VPNs do not make connected users anonymous to the ISP, and VPN providers may see user activity
Not every VPN supports split tunneling
Some protocols such as Windows native IKEv1 support are limited, and CIPE development ended in 2002
